title: KVarN: Variance-Normalized KV-Cache Quantization
hook: Long reasoning chains blow up the KV cache. Squeeze it to 2 bits and errors snowball over thousands of decode steps — unless you fix the token scales first.
key_points: Test-time scaling makes reasoning memory-bound: the KV cache grows with every decoded token.
Under autoregressive decoding, quantization errors *accumulate* across steps — unlike the prefill-style settings prior work tested.
The culprit is incorrect per-token scales; KVarN applies a Hadamard rotation plus dual-axis variance normalization to fix them.
Calibration-free, it sets a new state of the art for 2-bit KV-cache quantization on MATH500, AIME24, and HumanEval.
content_html: When a model "thinks" for a long time — the test-time scaling that drives modern reasoning — the bottleneck shifts from compute to memory. Every token decoded adds to the KV cache, and over thousands of steps that cache dominates memory. Quantizing it to very low precision is the obvious fix, but KVarN shows the standard evaluation has been misleading.
extra_html:
How it works

Prior KV-cache quantizers were largely measured in prefill-like settings, where the whole cache is quantized once. KVarN's key observation is that errors behave differently during long autoregressive decoding: they accumulate across timesteps, and the accumulation is driven primarily by incorrectly scaled tokens. The method is calibration-free — it applies a Hadamard rotation to the key and value matrices, then a dual-scaling variance normalization across both axes. Together these flatten outlying token-scale errors and sharply reduce the step-to-step error buildup.

Why it matters

At 2-bit precision, KVarN reports a new state of the art on generative reasoning benchmarks including MATH500, AIME24, and HumanEval, with a vLLM implementation released. The broader insight is that low-precision tricks validated on prefill don't automatically transfer to long-horizon decoding — the regime that reasoning models actually run in — and that controlling per-token scale is what keeps errors from compounding.

related.title: SmoothQuant: Accurate Post-Training Quantization for LLMs
related.hook: Activations are hard to quantize; weights are easy. SmoothQuant shifts that difficulty from activations into weights with a simple rescaling, enabling clean 8-bit inference.

related.hook: Generating one token reuses every prior key and value - that growing cache is why LLM inference is memory-bound, and continuous batching is how servers fight back.
